newsitem.title: UK: Mideast VLCC rates flat, no premium for new ships.
newsitem.headline: Mideast VLCC rates flat, no premium for new ships.

text.p: Middle East very large crude carrier (VLCC) rates ended the week little changed, with modern ships at no great advantage over older tonnage, brokers said.
"Modern tonnage fixing east was not able to demand any premium over its older rivals for fear of missing cargoes on their dates," said Galbraith's Ltd in their weekly tanker report.

Brokers E.A. Gibson said that "whilst we only anticipate 44 vessels of about 13 million tons being open within the next four weeks, the expected slowdown in fixing for March cargoes will do little to improve rates."
Mideast/west rates were flat at about W52.5, with South Korea and Singapore destinations at just under W60.
Galbraith's showed Middle East VLCC rates well below a year ago, with Mideast/Red Sea this week averaging W52.5 versus W72.5 this week last year, and Mideast Japan at W61.66 against W72.5.
West Africa/U.S. rates VLCC edged up over the week to about W72.5, with 130,000 tonne cargoes steady at about W105.
Galbraith's was bullish about the Suezmax (130,000 tonne) sector, saying, "Owners have not only been able to pick and choose which cargoes to offer for, but also which area they prefer to look at.
"The only thing that is surprising at the time of writing is that owners have not yet managed to push rates above W105 for West African cargoes and W105-110 for North Sea and Mediterranean loadings.
"They may well be saving their exertions for next week, since almost no VLCCs are available on their turf for charterers to use as a buffer or a fall-back position."

Med Aframax (80,000 tonne) cargoes remained at around W110, fluctuating five points up and down during the week, while inter-U.K./Cont they edged up only slightly to W125 despite strong activity, brokers said.
Caribs/upcoast 70,000 tonne vessels continued their climb on Friday on sustained demand, reaching W190/200 from W150 at the beginning of the week.
Inter-U.K./Cont and cross-Med 20,000 tonne fuel oil cargoes were both steady at W200.
